column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: In an experiment, what is the independent variable?
column14: A factor that is kept the same in every group
column15: The factor the scientist changes on purpose
column16: The factor the scientist measures to see what happened
column17: The group that gets no treatment at all
column28: The independent (manipulated) variable is the one factor the scientist changes on purpose, like the distance of a lamp. The factor that gets measured is the dependent variable, and that mix-up is the most common mistake.
column29: Think about which variable the scientist is in charge of setting.

column9: Which term names the factor that is measured or observed to see the effect of a change in an experiment?
column14: Independent variable
column15: Controlled variable
column16: Dependent variable
column17: Hypothesis
column28: The dependent (responding) variable is what you measure, such as bubbles per minute. It "depends" on the change you made. A common mistake is picking the independent variable, which is the factor you change.
column29: This variable responds to, or depends on, the change the scientist makes.

column9: Factors that are kept the same in every trial of an experiment are called ___ variables.
column28: Controlled variables (also called constants) are kept the same so they cannot affect the results. A common mistake is confusing them with the control group, which is a comparison group, not a variable.
column29: The scientist keeps these under control so they never change.

column9: A student puts sprigs of elodea 10 cm, 20 cm, and 30 cm from a lamp and counts the oxygen bubbles each one gives off per minute. What is the independent variable?
column14: The temperature of the water
column15: The number of bubbles per minute
column16: The distance from the lamp
column17: The type of plant
column28: The student changes the lamp distance on purpose, so distance is the independent variable. Bubbles per minute is what gets measured (the dependent variable), which is the most common wrong choice.
column29: Which factor did the student set to a different value for each sprig?

column9: Students grow radish seedlings under lamps of 20 W, 40 W, and 60 W. After two weeks, they measure the mass of the seedlings. What is the dependent variable?
column14: The mass of the seedlings
column15: The wattage of the lamps
column16: The kind of seeds planted
column17: The amount of water given each day
column28: The mass of the seedlings is what the students measure at the end, so it is the dependent variable. Lamp wattage is the independent variable they changed. Seed type and water should be kept the same (controlled).
column29: Look for the thing that gets measured at the end of the two weeks.

column9: A class tests whether the color of light affects how fast spinach leaf disks float. Which of these is a controlled variable?
column14: The color of the light
column15: The amount of baking soda solution in each cup
column16: Which color made the disks float first
column17: The time it takes the disks to float
column28: The amount of solution should be the same in every cup, so it is a controlled variable. The color of light is the independent variable, and the time to float is the dependent variable. Which color won is a result, not a variable.
column29: A controlled variable is something that should be identical in every cup.

column9: Which of these hypotheses could be tested with an experiment?
column14: Photosynthesis is the most important process on Earth.
column15: Plants enjoy sunlight more than they enjoy shade.
column16: If elodea gets more light, then it will give off more bubbles per minute.
column17: Plants are beautiful when they photosynthesize.
column28: A testable hypothesis names a change (more light) and a result you can measure (bubbles per minute). The other choices are opinions or feelings that no measurement can check, which is the most common mistake.
column29: Look for the statement with something you could change and something you could count.

column9: Why can counting the bubbles from an underwater plant be used to measure its rate of photosynthesis?
column14: The bubbles are made of the glucose the plant built
column15: The bubbles are oxygen, a product of photosynthesis, so more bubbles means faster photosynthesis
column16: The bubbles are carbon dioxide that the plant is pulling in from the water to use in photosynthesis
column17: The bubbles show that the water is starting to boil
column28: Photosynthesis releases oxygen, and an underwater plant gives it off as bubbles. The faster photosynthesis goes, the more bubbles per minute. A common mistake is thinking the bubbles are carbon dioxide, which the plant takes in, not gives off.
column29: Think about which gas photosynthesis gives off.

column9: What does the phrase "rate of photosynthesis" mean?
column14: How much photosynthesis happens in a set amount of time
column15: How tall a plant grows in its whole life
column16: The number of leaves on a plant
column17: The color of a plant's leaves
column28: A rate always compares an amount to time, like bubbles per minute. A common mistake is choosing plant size or height, which can depend on many things besides how fast photosynthesis is happening right now.
column29: The word rate is used in phrases like "miles per hour."

column9: Which piece of equipment would let a student change the light intensity in an elodea experiment most easily?
column14: A balance
column15: A lamp that can be moved closer or farther away
column16: A graduated cylinder
column17: A thermometer
column28: Moving a lamp closer or farther changes how much light reaches the plant. A thermometer measures temperature, a balance measures mass, and a graduated cylinder measures volume; none of them change the light.
column29: Which tool makes light in the first place?

column9: Select every factor that can change the rate of photosynthesis. Select all that apply.
column14: Temperature
column15: Light intensity
column16: The day of the week the lab is done
column17: Color (wavelength) of light
column19: The height of the student doing the lab
column28: Light intensity, light color, carbon dioxide, and temperature all affect photosynthesis. The student's height and the day of the week have nothing to do with the chemistry inside a chloroplast. A common mistake is leaving out light color.
column29: Think about the raw materials and conditions a chloroplast needs.

column9: A student moves a lamp farther away from a beaker of elodea. What happens to the light intensity that reaches the plant?
column14: It increases
column15: It stays exactly the same
column16: It changes into carbon dioxide
column17: It decreases
column28: Light spreads out as it travels, so the farther the lamp is, the less light reaches the plant. A common mistake is thinking distance does not matter as long as the lamp is on.
column29: Think about how bright a flashlight looks from across a football field.

column9: In an elodea lab where the lamp distance is changed, the number of oxygen bubbles counted each minute is the ___ variable.
column28: Bubbles per minute is what gets measured, so it is the dependent (responding) variable. A common mistake is calling it independent; the lamp distance is the independent variable.
column29: Is the bubble count something the student sets, or something the student measures?

column9: In an experiment testing how the color of light affects photosynthesis, the color of the light is the ___ variable.
column28: The scientist chooses the light color on purpose, so it is the independent (manipulated) variable. A common mistake is calling it dependent because it is the main topic of the experiment.
column29: Who decides the color, the scientist or the plant?

column9: What is the purpose of a control group in an experiment?
column14: It is the group that gets the biggest change
column15: It proves that the hypothesis is correct
column16: It gives a normal comparison for the groups that get the change
column17: It makes the experiment finish faster
column28: A control group is left normal, so you can compare it with the groups that were changed. Without it you cannot tell whether the change made any difference. A common mistake is thinking the control group proves the hypothesis.
column29: You need something to compare against.

column9: Students want to know whether red light makes elodea give off more bubbles than ordinary white light. Which setup should they use for comparison (the control)?
column14: A cactus under the white light
column15: Elodea in a dark closet in warm water
column16: Elodea under red light with the lamp twice as far away, so the light is less bright
column17: Elodea under white light at the same distance and water temperature
column28: The question compares red light with normal white light, so the control is elodea under white light with everything else the same. Changing the distance, temperature, or kind of plant adds extra variables, which is the most common mistake.
column29: The control should match the test setup in every way except the one thing being tested.

column9: Why do scientists run several trials of the same experiment?
column14: To make sure the results match what they predicted before the experiment
column15: To use up all of the lab materials
column16: To test a different independent variable each time the experiment is repeated
column17: To make the results more reliable and catch mistakes or odd results
column28: Repeating trials shows whether a result happens again and again, and it helps you spot an odd result caused by a mistake. A common mistake is thinking trials are done to get the "right" answer; scientists report what they find even if it does not match the prediction.
column29: If you got a result only once, how sure could you be?

column9: When you graph the results of an experiment, which variable usually goes on the x-axis (the horizontal axis)?
column14: The dependent variable
column15: The controlled variables
column16: The independent variable
column17: The number of trials
column28: The independent variable (what you changed) goes on the x-axis, and the dependent variable (what you measured) goes on the y-axis. Swapping the two axes is the most common graphing mistake.
column29: The variable you choose comes first, along the bottom.

column9: Elodea data: lamp at 10 cm gave 32 bubbles per minute, 20 cm gave 21, 30 cm gave 12, and 40 cm gave 6. Which statement describes the trend?
column14: As the lamp moves farther away, the number of bubbles increases
column15: The lamp distance has no effect on the number of bubbles
column16: As the lamp moves farther away, the number of bubbles decreases
column17: The number of bubbles stays the same until 40 cm
column28: As the distance goes up (10 to 40 cm), the bubbles go down (32 to 6). Less light reaches the plant from far away, so photosynthesis slows. A common mistake is reading only the distance column, which goes up.
column29: Read both columns together: when distance gets bigger, what happens to the bubbles?

column9: A student counts the bubbles from a sprig of cabomba, an aquarium plant, for one minute in four trials: 18, 22, 20, and 24 bubbles. What is the mean (average) number of bubbles per minute?
column28: Mean = (18 + 22 + 20 + 24) ÷ 4 = 84 ÷ 4 = 21 bubbles per minute. A common mistake is dividing by 3 instead of the number of trials, which is 4.
column29: Add all four counts, then divide by how many trials there were.

column9: Which of these is a quantitative (number-based) measurement of photosynthesis?
column14: The leaves look healthy and bright
column15: The plant looks greener than before
column16: The water seems a little cloudier
column17: 15 oxygen bubbles per minute
column28: A quantitative measurement is a number with a unit, like 15 bubbles per minute. The other choices are qualitative descriptions that depend on opinion, which is the common mistake.
column29: Quantitative sounds like quantity, an amount you can count.

column9: Two cups of spinach leaf disks are placed under lamps. The disks in Cup A float after 8 minutes. The disks in Cup B float after 20 minutes. Which cup had the faster rate of photosynthesis?
column14: Cup B, because a longer time means more photosynthesis
column15: Cup A, because oxygen built up in its disks faster
column16: Both cups had the same rate because all the disks floated
column17: Neither cup, because floating disks are not doing photosynthesis
column28: Disks float when oxygen from photosynthesis builds up inside them. The cup whose disks float in less time is making oxygen faster. A common mistake is thinking the bigger number (20 minutes) means more photosynthesis.
column29: Think of a race: is the winner the one with the shortest time or the longest time?

column9: Which statement best describes how temperature affects photosynthesis?
column14: Photosynthesis works fastest near the freezing point of water
column15: Temperature has no effect, because only light matters
column16: The rate rises as temperature goes up to a certain point, then drops if it gets too hot
column17: The hotter it gets, the faster photosynthesis goes, because heat always speeds up reactions
column28: Photosynthesis depends on enzymes. Warmth speeds them up to a point, but too much heat damages them and the rate falls. A common mistake is thinking hotter is always better.
column29: Enzymes are proteins. What happens to proteins like egg whites when they get too hot?

column9: Why should an experiment change only one variable at a time?
column14: So any change in the results can be linked to that one variable
column15: So the experiment uses less equipment
column16: So the results will match the hypothesis
column17: So the dependent variable does not change
column28: If only one thing is different between groups, that one thing must be the cause of any difference in the results. If two things change, you cannot tell which one caused it. A common mistake is thinking the goal is to get the expected result.
column29: If you changed two things and the result changed, which one gets the credit?

column9: Which question could be answered by doing an experiment?
column14: Is elodea the prettiest pond plant?
column15: Does the amount of light affect how many bubbles elodea gives off per minute?
column16: Should every classroom have a plant?
column17: Which lamp color looks the nicest?
column28: A testable question has something you can change (amount of light) and something you can measure (bubbles per minute). Questions about what is prettiest, nicest, or what people should do are opinions, which is the common mistake.
column29: Can you measure the answer with a number?

column9: A student tests whether warming the water to 30 °C changes how much oxygen elodea makes, compared with tubes left at room temperature (20 °C). The lamp is kept 20 cm away from every tube. Match each part of the experiment to its role.
column14: Water temperature :: Independent variable
column15: Volume of oxygen collected in 10 minutes :: Dependent variable
column16: Lamp kept 20 cm away from every tube :: Controlled variable
column17: Tubes left at room temperature (20 °C) :: Control group
column28: The student changes the water temperature (independent), measures oxygen volume (dependent), keeps the lamp distance the same (controlled), and compares against the normal room-temperature tubes (control group). A common mistake is calling the control group a controlled variable.
column29: Start with the factor the student changed on purpose, then find what was measured.

column9: Which tool measures light intensity directly?
column14: A thermometer
column15: A balance
column16: A light meter
column17: A graduated cylinder
column28: A light meter measures how much light hits a spot (often in lux). A thermometer measures temperature, a balance measures mass, and a graduated cylinder measures volume.
column29: The tool's name includes the thing it measures.

column9: Students test elodea under red, blue, green, and white light and record the bubbles per minute for each. Which type of graph best shows these results?
column14: A bar graph, because the light colors are separate categories
column15: A line graph, because the colors are connected to each other in a rainbow
column16: A pie graph, because the colors add up to 100%
column17: No graph, because colors cannot be graphed
column28: Light colors are separate groups, not numbers on a scale, so a bar graph fits. A line graph is used when the independent variable is a number that changes smoothly, like distance or temperature, and that is the common mix-up.
column29: Is "red, blue, green, white" a set of numbers or a set of groups?

column9: When one factor is in short supply and holds back the rate of photosynthesis even though the other factors are plentiful, it is called a ___ factor.
column28: A limiting factor is the one in shortest supply; it sets the top speed. Adding more of the other factors will not help until the limiting factor is increased. A common mistake is calling it the controlled variable.
column29: It puts a limit on how fast the process can go.

column9: Why should every elodea sprig in an experiment be about the same size?
column14: Because sprig size is the dependent variable, the thing the student measures at the end of the lab
column15: So the experiment looks neat in photos
column16: A bigger sprig has more leaves and could give off more bubbles anyway, making the test unfair
column17: So the sprigs all fit in the same beaker
column28: More leaves means more chloroplasts and more bubbles, even under the same light. If sprig sizes differ, size becomes a second variable. Size is a controlled variable, not the dependent variable, which is the common mistake.
column29: If one sprig is twice as big, what would you expect from its bubble count?

column9: If an experiment's results do not support the hypothesis, the experiment was a failure and should be thrown out.
column28: False. Results that do not support the hypothesis are still useful; they tell you something real about how photosynthesis works. Scientists report them and may revise the hypothesis. The common mistake is thinking only "correct" predictions count.
column29: Do scientists learn anything when a prediction turns out wrong?

column9: A greenhouse near Cadott runs a heater in January so the air stays at 24 °C even when it is −10 °C outside. Which factor affecting photosynthesis is the grower controlling?
column14: Light intensity
column15: Temperature
column16: Light color
column17: Carbon dioxide level
column28: The heater keeps the temperature in a range where the plant's enzymes work well. It does not change light or carbon dioxide. A common mistake is thinking a heater adds light.
column29: What does a heater change?

column9: Which change would most likely DECREASE the rate of photosynthesis for a houseplant sitting on a sunny windowsill?
column14: Giving it a normal amount of water
column15: Opening the window to let in fresh air
column16: Cleaning the dust off its leaves
column17: Moving it to a dark hallway
column28: Moving the plant to a dark hallway cuts its light, so photosynthesis slows. Watering, fresh air (carbon dioxide), and clean leaves would keep the rate up or help it. The common mistake is overlooking the word DECREASE.
column29: Which choice takes away something the plant needs?

column9: Which unit fits a rate of photosynthesis measured in an elodea lab?
column14: Degrees Celsius
column15: Watts
column16: Centimeters
column17: Bubbles per minute
column28: A rate compares an amount to time, so bubbles per minute fits. Centimeters could be the lamp distance, degrees Celsius the water temperature, and watts the bulb power; those describe the setup, not the rate.
column29: A rate is always "something per something."

column9: Chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light. A student puts elodea under green light of the same brightness as a white lamp. Compared with white light, what should she predict?
column14: More bubbles, because leaves are green
column15: The same number of bubbles, because light color does not matter if the brightness is the same
column16: Fewer bubbles, because chlorophyll absorbs little green light and reflects much of it
column17: No bubbles at all, because green light is not real light
column28: Chlorophyll absorbs little green light, and light that is not absorbed cannot power photosynthesis, so the rate drops (but usually not all the way to zero). A common mistake is thinking green leaves use green light best.
column29: The color a leaf looks is the color it bounces back.

column9: A student tests how light intensity affects bubbles from elodea. Select every variable that should be kept the same in every trial. Select all that apply.
column14: Amount of baking soda in the water
column15: Number of bubbles counted
column16: Distance from the lamp
column17: Water temperature
column28: Temperature, baking soda, sprig size, and kind of plant should all stay the same. The lamp distance is how the light intensity is changed (independent variable), and the bubble count is the dependent variable. Choosing the lamp distance is the most common mistake.
column29: Rule out the one thing being changed and the one thing being measured.

column9: In the floating leaf disk lab, what is usually measured as the dependent variable?
column14: The number of disks floating over time (or the time for them to float)
column15: The size of the cup
column16: The color of the lamp
column17: The kind of leaf the disks came from
column28: Students count how many disks float each minute, or time how long they take to rise, because floating shows that oxygen is building up. The lamp, cup, and kind of leaf are parts of the setup that should be kept the same or changed on purpose.
column29: What do you write down every minute during the leaf disk lab?

column9: Why should a student keep a lamp's cord and plug away from the beaker of water during an elodea lab?
column14: Water and electricity together can cause a shock
column15: The cord blocks the light from the lamp
column16: The cord makes extra bubbles in the water
column17: The cord cools the water down
column28: Spilled water touching a plug or cord can cause an electric shock. Safe setups keep electrical parts dry and away from containers of water. The other choices are not real effects of a lamp cord.
column29: What is the danger when water meets electricity?

column9: To check that the water temperature stays the same in every trial of an elodea experiment, a student should use a ___.
column28: A thermometer (or a temperature probe) measures the water temperature, so the student can make sure it stays controlled. A common mistake is naming a light meter, which measures light, not heat.
column29: This tool's name starts with "thermo-," which means heat.

column9: Elodea gave off 12 bubbles per minute with the lamp at 30 cm and 30 bubbles per minute with the lamp at 10 cm. How many more bubbles per minute did it give off at 10 cm?
column28: 30 − 12 = 18 more bubbles per minute at 10 cm. A common mistake is subtracting the distances (30 − 10) instead of the bubble counts.
column29: Subtract the smaller bubble count from the larger one.

column9: A student counts 14 bubbles from an elodea sprig in 30 seconds. What is the rate in bubbles per minute?
column28: 30 seconds is half a minute, so the rate is 14 × 2 = 28 bubbles per minute. A common mistake is reporting 14, which is bubbles per half minute, or dividing by 2 to get 7.
column29: How many 30-second periods are in one minute?

column9: Which plant would be BEST for an experiment that counts oxygen bubbles?
column14: A cactus in a pot of dry sand
column15: A large oak tree
column16: An underwater plant such as elodea
column17: A mushroom growing on a log
column28: Bubbles can only be seen when the oxygen is released under water, so an underwater plant like elodea works well. A cactus and an oak release oxygen into air where you cannot see it, and a mushroom is a fungus that does not do photosynthesis at all.
column29: Where would you be able to see a gas come out as bubbles?

column9: A Wisconsin farmer waters half of a cornfield with irrigation and leaves the other half with rain only. In the fall, she compares how many bushels of corn each half produces. What is the independent variable?
column14: The bushels of corn produced
column15: The weather in the fall
column16: The type of corn planted
column17: The amount of water the corn gets
column28: The farmer chose which half gets extra water, so the amount of water is the independent variable. The bushels produced is the dependent variable, the most common wrong choice.
column29: Which factor did the farmer decide on before the corn grew?

column9: In the elodea lab, a student counts bubbles for exactly one minute at each lamp distance. Why should she use the same amount of time for every count?
column14: So the lamp does not burn out
column15: Because elodea only makes bubbles for about one minute after the lamp is first turned on
column16: So the water stays the same color
column17: So counts are fair to compare; a longer count would give more bubbles at the same rate
column28: Counting for 2 minutes instead of 1 would roughly double the count even if the rate stayed the same. Keeping the time the same makes the counts fair to compare. A common mistake is thinking the time is just for convenience.
column29: What would happen to the count if you counted twice as long?

column9: On a sunny summer day, where in Lake Wissota would algae most likely have the highest rate of photosynthesis?
column14: Near the sunny surface of the water
column15: In the shade under a covered boat dock
column16: Inside a dark drainage pipe that empties into the lake
column17: At the dark bottom of the deepest part of the lake
column28: Light is brightest near the surface, so algae there can photosynthesize fastest. Water absorbs light as you go deeper, and docks and pipes block it. A common mistake is thinking algae everywhere in the lake get the same light.
column29: Which spot gets the most light?

column9: A student wants to test whether water temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis in elodea. Which is the best hypothesis?
column14: Temperature is one of the factors in photosynthesis.
column15: If the lamp is made brighter, then the elodea will give off more bubbles per minute, because it gets more light energy
column16: Elodea will give off bubbles during the experiment.
column17: If the water warms from 10 °C to 25 °C, then elodea will give off more bubbles per minute, because enzymes speed up
column28: The best hypothesis names the independent variable (water temperature), the dependent variable (bubbles per minute), and a reason. One choice tests light instead of temperature, which is a common mix-up, and the others are not predictions that link a change to a result.
column29: Look for an "If ..., then ..., because ..." statement about the right variable.

column9: A student moves a hot incandescent lamp closer to a beaker of elodea, and the water warms from 21 °C to 27 °C. Why is this a problem for her experiment?
column14: Warm water has no effect on photosynthesis, so it is not a problem
column15: Light and temperature both changed, so she cannot tell which one caused the change in bubbles
column16: The heat makes the bubbles impossible to count
column17: The plant will stop making oxygen as soon as the water warms at all, so there will be no bubbles
column28: When two variables change together, either one could explain the result. Here light intensity and temperature both went up. A common mistake is thinking temperature does not matter, but warming speeds up the enzymes for photosynthesis.
column29: Count how many things were different between the trials.

column9: After moving a lamp to a new distance, a student waits 3 minutes before she starts counting elodea bubbles. What is the best reason for waiting?
column14: So bubbles from the last trial can be counted again
column15: Because elodea only makes bubbles every three minutes, so a shorter wait would show zero bubbles
column16: So the plant can rest and use up its oxygen
column17: To let the plant adjust to the new light level, so the count shows the rate at that level
column28: A plant's rate does not change instantly when the light changes. Waiting lets the rate settle so the count reflects the new distance and not the old one. A common mistake is starting the count right away, which mixes two light levels in one count.
column29: Does the plant's bubbling speed up the instant the lamp moves?

column9: Students test elodea under lamps of 25 W, 60 W, and 100 W. Their teacher suggests adding one more tube of elodea that sits in the dark. What does that tube add to the experiment?
column14: A baseline that shows how many bubbles appear without light, for comparison
column15: A way to measure the water temperature
column16: A second independent variable that can be tested at the same time as the lamp wattage
column17: Extra bubbles that make the bright tubes go faster
column28: The dark tube is a control. If it gives off few or no bubbles, it shows the bubbles in the lit tubes really come from light-driven photosynthesis. A common mistake is thinking the control is a second variable being tested.
column29: What would you compare the lit tubes against?

column9: A student's elodea experiment gave strange results. Select every problem that would make her results unreliable. Select all that apply.
column14: She kept the water temperature the same for every trial
column15: She used the same lamp for every trial
column16: She used a big sprig at one distance and a tiny sprig at another
column17: She did only one trial at each distance
column18: She counted bubbles for 1 minute at some distances and 2 minutes at others
column28: Different sprig sizes and different counting times add extra variables, and a single trial cannot show whether a result is typical. Keeping temperature the same and using the same lamp are good practices, not problems; picking them is the common mistake.
column29: Look for anything that was NOT kept fair or was not repeated.

column9: An oxygen sensor in a sealed chamber with spinach leaves reads 4.0% oxygen at the start and 5.2% after 6 minutes under a lamp. What is the average rate of increase, in percent per minute?
column28: Change = 5.2 − 4.0 = 1.2%. Rate = 1.2 ÷ 6 = 0.2% per minute. A common mistake is dividing 5.2 by 6 without first finding how much the oxygen changed.
column29: First find how much the oxygen went up, then divide by the minutes.

column9: Elodea gave off 20 bubbles per minute under a 40 W bulb and 30 bubbles per minute under a 100 W bulb at the same distance. By what percent did the rate increase?
column28: Percent change = (30 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 10 ÷ 20 × 100 = 50%. A common mistake is dividing by the new value (30), which gives about 33%.
column29: Find the change, divide by the starting value, then multiply by 100.

column9: A gas syringe collects 3.6 mL of oxygen from a pondweed sprig in 12 minutes. What is the rate in mL per minute?
column28: Rate = 3.6 mL ÷ 12 min = 0.3 mL per minute. A common mistake is dividing 12 by 3.6, which flips the rate upside down.
column29: Divide the amount of gas by the time.

column9: A hypothesis says, "If the temperature increases, then elodea will make more bubbles." The results were 5 bubbles per minute at 10 °C, 11 at 20 °C, and 17 at 30 °C. Which conclusion is best?
column14: The data prove that elodea makes more bubbles at every temperature, no matter how hot
column15: The data support the hypothesis for temperatures between 10 °C and 30 °C
column16: The data do not support the hypothesis, because the numbers changed
column17: No conclusion can be made, because bubbles are not related to photosynthesis
column28: Bubbles rose each time the temperature rose, so the data support the hypothesis, but only for the range tested. A common mistake is overclaiming: this experiment says nothing about much hotter water, where enzymes can be damaged.
column29: A good conclusion only talks about the temperatures that were actually tested.

column9: Students want to know whether light intensity affects photosynthesis in elodea. Which plan is the best experimental design?
column14: Put identical sprigs 10, 20, 30, and 40 cm from one lamp, keep all else the same, and count bubbles, 3 trials each
column15: Put sprigs at different distances from the lamp, count once, and use a different kind of water plant at each distance
column16: Change both the lamp distance and the water temperature in each trial so more factors get tested at once
column17: Put one sprig by a window and one in a closet, then look at them once the next day
column28: The best plan changes only the lamp distance, controls the other variables, measures a number (bubbles per minute), and repeats trials. Changing two things at once or using different plants adds extra variables, which is the most common design mistake.
column29: Look for the plan that changes one thing, measures a number, and repeats.

column9: Cup A has leaf disks in baking soda solution under a bright lamp. Cup B has disks in plain water on a dim shelf. Cup A's disks float first. The student concludes that baking soda speeds up photosynthesis. Why is this conclusion weak?
column14: The light differed too, so the brighter lamp could explain the faster floating instead of baking soda
column15: Baking soda has nothing to do with photosynthesis
column16: Leaf disks never float in plain water under any light
column17: Cup A should have floated last if baking soda really helps photosynthesis, so the result is backwards
column28: Two things differed between the cups: carbon dioxide (baking soda) and light. Either one could explain the result. To test baking soda, both cups need the same lamp at the same distance. A common mistake is assuming the variable you care about must be the cause.
column29: List every way the two cups were different.

column9: Put the steps of designing and running a photosynthesis experiment in order.
column14: Collect data in a table over several trials
column15: Ask a testable question, such as whether light color affects bubbles per minute
column16: Analyze the data and write a conclusion about the hypothesis
column17: Write a hypothesis that predicts the result
column18: Set up groups that differ in only the independent variable
column28: A scientist asks a question, predicts an answer (hypothesis), sets up a fair test, collects data, then analyzes it to judge the hypothesis. A common mistake is writing the conclusion before collecting data, or skipping the hypothesis.
column29: You cannot predict an answer before you have a question.

column9: Put the steps of an elodea light-intensity experiment in order.
column14: Count the bubbles for 1 minute and record the number
column15: Move the lamp to the next distance and repeat the count
column16: Set the lamp at the first distance and wait a few minutes
column17: Cut the stem of a fresh elodea sprig and place it in a test tube of water with a little baking soda
column18: Average the trials for each distance and make a graph
column28: Set up the plant first, then set the light and let the plant adjust, count and record, change the distance and repeat, and finally average and graph. A common mistake is graphing before all the distances have been tested.
column29: The plant has to be set up before anything can be counted.

column9: Match each lab observation to what it detects.
column14: Counting bubbles from elodea :: Oxygen being released
column15: BTB changing from yellow back to blue :: Carbon dioxide being used up
column16: Leaf disks rising in a cup of solution :: Oxygen building up inside the leaf tissue
column17: Iodine turning blue-black on a leaf :: Starch made from the plant's glucose
column28: Bubbles and rising disks both show oxygen, but bubbles are oxygen leaving the plant while disks rise because oxygen collects inside them. BTB turns blue as carbon dioxide is removed, and iodine detects starch. A common mistake is thinking BTB detects oxygen.
column29: Two of these detect the same gas in different ways. Decide which one is the gas leaving and which is the gas trapped inside.

column9: A coleus leaf has green areas and white areas with no chlorophyll. After a day in sunlight, the leaf is tested with iodine, which turns blue-black where starch is present. What result is expected?
column14: No part turns blue-black, because coleus does not store starch
column15: The whole leaf turns blue-black, because the whole leaf was in the sun
column16: Only the white areas turn blue-black, because they reflect the most light and store the extra energy
column17: Only green areas turn blue-black, since only parts with chlorophyll make sugar to store as starch
column28: Chlorophyll captures the light energy for photosynthesis, so only the green areas make glucose and store it as starch. A common mistake is thinking sunlight alone is enough, even where there is no chlorophyll.
column29: Which parts of the leaf have the pigment that captures light?

column9: In a leaf disk lab, Group 1 tested one disk per cup. Group 2 tested 10 disks per cup. Everything else was the same. Whose results are more trustworthy, and why?
column14: Group 1, because using fewer disks means there is less chance of making an error
column15: Group 1, because one disk is easier to watch
column16: Both are equally trustworthy, since they used the same lamp and the same solution
column17: Group 2, because with more disks one unusual disk has less effect on the result
column28: A larger sample size means one odd disk (a torn one, or one with an air bubble) cannot change the result much. With one disk, the whole result depends on that single disk. A common mistake is thinking less data means fewer errors.
column29: If one disk was damaged, which group would be thrown off more?

column9: Four trials with the lamp at 20 cm gave 18, 19, 41, and 17 bubbles per minute. What should the student do about the 41?
column14: Throw out all four trials and stop the experiment
column15: Use only the 41, because it is the biggest number
column16: Treat it as a possible error, look for what went wrong, and repeat that trial
column17: Change the other three numbers to match 41
column28: A value far from the others is an outlier that may come from a mistake, like counting for too long or a different sprig. Checking and repeating the trial is honest and keeps the average from being pulled up. Changing data to match is never allowed, which is the key mistake to avoid.
column29: Does 41 look like it belongs with the other three?

column9: Select every change that would INCREASE the light intensity reaching a plant. Select all that apply.
column14: Move the lamp closer to the plant
column15: Warm the water around the plant
column16: Add baking soda to the water
column17: Move the lamp farther from the plant
column18: Switch to a brighter bulb of the same type
column19: Remove a shade cloth that was covering the plant
column28: Moving the lamp closer, using a brighter bulb, and removing shade all put more light on the plant. Baking soda adds carbon dioxide and warming changes temperature; both can affect photosynthesis, but neither changes light intensity, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Only pick the changes that put more light on the leaves.

column9: Which graph shape would you expect for bubbles per minute (y-axis) against light intensity (x-axis), from darkness up to very bright light?
column14: A flat line that never changes
column15: It rises, then levels off
column16: It starts high and falls steadily
column17: A straight line that keeps rising forever
column28: At first, more light means more photosynthesis, so the line rises. In very bright light, something else, like carbon dioxide or temperature, becomes limiting and the line levels off. A common mistake is thinking more light always means more photosynthesis.
column29: Can a plant keep speeding up forever just from more light?

column9: A student wants to test how carbon dioxide concentration affects how fast leaf disks float. Which set of cups is the best design?
column14: Every cup with the same amount of baking soda, but each under a different brightness of lamp
column15: Cups with different amounts of baking soda, each holding disks from a different kind of leaf
column16: Cups with 0 g, 0.5 g, 1 g, and 2 g of baking soda, each in the same volume of water
column17: One cup with baking soda and one cup with vinegar
column28: Baking soda adds carbon dioxide, so different amounts in the same volume of water change only the carbon dioxide level. Vinegar adds a new chemical, different lamps change light, and different leaves add another variable, which are the common mistakes.
column29: Only the carbon dioxide source should differ between the cups.

column9: Minutes for half of the leaf disks to float: lamp at 10 cm, 9 minutes; 20 cm, 14 minutes; 40 cm, 26 minutes. Which statement is correct?
column14: Photosynthesis was the same at every distance, because the disks floated every single time
column15: Photosynthesis was fastest at 40 cm, because it has the biggest number
column16: The lamp distance had no effect, because the times all went up
column17: Photosynthesis was fastest at 10 cm, because the disks floated in the shortest time
column28: A shorter time to float means oxygen built up faster, so the rate was highest at 10 cm, where the light was brightest. A common mistake is treating the largest number as the fastest rate; here the numbers are times, not counts.
column29: Is a smaller time a sign of a faster or a slower process?

column9: Counting bubbles for a longer time, such as 5 minutes, and then dividing to find bubbles per minute can make a rate measurement more accurate.
column28: True. Over a longer count, a few missed or extra bubbles make up a smaller share of the total, so the per-minute rate is more accurate. A common mistake is thinking a 5-minute count gives a rate five times bigger; you divide by 5 to get bubbles per minute.
column29: Would one miscounted bubble matter more in a count of 10 or a count of 50?

column9: Students measure the dissolved oxygen in a pond at 6 a.m. and again at 4 p.m. on a sunny day. What do they most likely find, and why?
column14: The same amount both times, because plants make oxygen at a steady rate all day and night
column15: More oxygen at 4 p.m., because algae and plants photosynthesized all day in the light
column16: No oxygen at either time, because ponds do not have dissolved oxygen
column17: More oxygen at 6 a.m., because plants make the most oxygen at night
column28: During the day, light lets algae and plants photosynthesize and add oxygen to the water. Overnight, there is no photosynthesis but respiration keeps using oxygen, so it is lowest at dawn. A common mistake is thinking plants make oxygen at night.
column29: Which time comes after many hours of sunlight?

column9: Elodea gave off 8 bubbles per minute under green light and 24 bubbles per minute under blue light of the same brightness. How many times faster was the rate under blue light?
column28: 24 ÷ 8 = 3, so the blue-light rate was 3 times faster. A common mistake is subtracting (24 − 8 = 16), which tells how many more bubbles, not how many times faster.
column29: "How many times" means divide, not subtract.

column9: A student wants to test whether the amount of light affects how fast grass grows. Which plan controls the other variables best?
column14: Use one pot and move it to a new spot each day
column15: Plant a different kind of grass in each pot so more types are tested, and give each pot the same water
column16: Identical pots, seeds, soil, and water, with shade cloths that block 0%, 30%, and 60% of the light
column17: Water the pot in full sun more often because it dries out faster, and keep the other pots in the shade
column28: Everything is the same except the amount of light, which is set by the shade cloths. Watering one pot more adds water as a second variable, which is the sneakiest mistake. Different grasses or one moving pot also make the test unfair.
column29: Find the plan where light is the only difference between pots.

column9: Which result would NOT support the hypothesis "If light intensity increases, then the rate of photosynthesis increases"?
column14: Oxygen collected in 10 minutes went up as the lamp moved closer
column15: Bubbles per minute went from 4 to 9 to 15 as the light got brighter
column16: Leaf disks floated faster under the brighter lamp
column17: Bubbles per minute stayed about the same at every light intensity
column28: If brighter light does not change the rate, the data do not support the hypothesis. The other three all show the rate going up with more light. A common mistake is missing the word NOT in the question.
column29: Three of these show the rate going up. Find the one that does not.

column9: Pond plants have plenty of light and carbon dioxide, but on a cold spring morning their rate of photosynthesis is still very low. The factor most likely holding back their photosynthesis is ___.
column28: With light and carbon dioxide plentiful, the cold is what slows the enzymes, so temperature is the limiting factor. A common mistake is naming light because it is the factor people think of first.
column29: Which factor in the description is not at a good level?

column9: The temperature at which an enzyme-driven process like photosynthesis runs fastest is called its ___ temperature.
column28: The optimum temperature is where enzymes work fastest. Below it, molecules move slowly; far above it, the enzymes lose their shape. A common mistake is thinking the hottest temperature tested is always the optimum.
column29: It is a word that means "best" or "most favorable."

column9: A student tests how the number of leaves on an elodea sprig (2, 4, or 6 leaves) affects bubbles per minute. The lamp, water temperature, and baking soda are kept the same. In this experiment, the number of leaves is the ___ variable.
column28: The student sets the number of leaves on purpose, so it is the independent variable here. In other elodea experiments sprig size is kept the same, so students often call it a controlled variable; what matters is the role it plays in THIS experiment.
column29: Did the student choose the number of leaves, or measure it?

column9: In an elodea experiment, the tube with the lamp turned off gave 0 bubbles per minute, while the lit tubes gave many. What does the 0 tell the student?
column14: The bubbles need light, so they likely come from photosynthesis, not from something like warming water
column15: The tube with no light was set up wrong and must be thrown out, because every elodea tube should make bubbles
column16: The elodea in that tube must have died
column17: Light has nothing to do with the bubbles
column28: If bubbles stop when the light is off, the light is needed for them, which points to photosynthesis. The result is a useful control, not a mistake. A common mistake is thinking a zero means the plant died; it starts bubbling again when the light returns.
column29: What is the only difference between the dark tube and the lit tubes?

column9: Elodea is in 15 °C water with plenty of baking soda. As the lamp brightness is turned up through five settings, the bubbles per minute are 2, 10, 18, 21, and 21. Which change would most likely raise the rate above 21?
column14: Move the lamp farther away
column15: Turn the light up even brighter, past the last setting, to give the plant more energy
column16: Count the bubbles for a shorter time so the count is easier to keep track of
column17: Warm the water toward about 25 °C while keeping the bright light
column28: The rate leveled off, so light is no longer the limiting factor. Carbon dioxide is already plentiful, which leaves the cool 15 °C water as the most likely limit. A common mistake is adding even more light after the graph has leveled off.
column29: When more light stops helping, look for the factor that is still at a poor level.

column9: Elodea bubbles per minute: low light with no baking soda, 4; low light with baking soda, 5; bright light with no baking soda, 9; bright light with baking soda, 22. What do these results show?
column14: Light has no effect, because the baking soda made all the difference
column15: Carbon dioxide was the limiting factor in low light
column16: Light was the limiting factor in low light, so carbon dioxide helped a lot only in bright light
column17: Baking soda always doubles the rate, no matter how much light there is, so light does not matter
column28: In low light, baking soda barely changed the rate (4 to 5), so light was holding it back. In bright light, baking soda more than doubled it (9 to 22), so carbon dioxide had become the limit. A common mistake is reading only one row of the data.
column29: Compare the effect of baking soda in low light with its effect in bright light.

column9: A student notices that lawns on the south side of houses turn green and grow faster in spring than lawns on the north side. He concludes, "More sunlight causes faster grass growth." Which is the best critique?
column14: He should have looked at the lawns at night instead
column15: Grass does not do photosynthesis, so light cannot matter
column16: South-side lawns may also be warmer and drier, so a controlled test that changes only light is needed
column17: His conclusion is already proven, because south sides always get more sun and the grass there grew faster
column28: Sunny south sides also get warmer and may have different soil moisture, so temperature or water could explain the growth. An observation like this is a good starting point for a hypothesis, but only a controlled test can show cause. A common mistake is treating a pattern as proof.
column29: Besides light, what else is different about the south side of a house?

column9: Sprig A has a mass of 2.0 g and gives off 30 bubbles per minute. Sprig B has a mass of 5.0 g and gives off 60 bubbles per minute. To compare them fairly, what is Sprig B's rate in bubbles per minute per gram?
column28: 60 ÷ 5.0 = 12 bubbles per minute per gram. (Sprig A is 30 ÷ 2.0 = 15, so for its size Sprig A is actually faster.) A common mistake is comparing the raw counts, which makes the bigger sprig look faster just because it has more leaves.
column29: Divide the bubbles per minute by the sprig's mass.

column9: A graph shows oxygen made by a plant (y-axis) against carbon dioxide level (x-axis) at 15 °C and at 25 °C. Both lines rise and then level off, but the 25 °C line levels off much higher. What is the best conclusion?
column14: Temperature only matters when carbon dioxide is very low, and it stops mattering once the lines level off
column15: Carbon dioxide has no effect on photosynthesis
column16: With plenty of carbon dioxide, temperature became the limit, so warmer plants reached a higher top rate
column17: The 15 °C plants were given less light, so the test is useless
column28: Both lines rise at first, so carbon dioxide matters. Where they flatten, more carbon dioxide stops helping; the only difference between the lines is temperature, so temperature set the maximum rate. A common mistake is thinking temperature matters only at low carbon dioxide, which is the opposite of what the graph shows.
column29: Look at where the lines flatten. What is the only difference between the two lines?

column9: Which design tests the effect of temperature on photosynthesis in elodea most fairly?
column14: Put one tube in a dark refrigerator and one on a sunny windowsill
column15: Identical sprigs in 10, 20, 30, and 40 °C water baths, same LED lamp, distance, and baking soda; count bubbles, 3 trials
column16: Use a hot incandescent lamp at different distances to heat each tube to a different temperature, 3 trials each
column17: Heat the water to 40 °C, then count bubbles as it cools, moving the lamp closer as it cools so bubbles are easier to see
column28: Water baths set the temperature without changing the light, and the same LED lamp keeps light controlled. Using lamp distance to heat the water, a dark fridge, or moving the lamp all change light along with temperature, which is the most common design flaw.
column29: In a fair temperature test, the light must be the same in every tube.

column9: A student concluded, "Blue light causes the most photosynthesis in all plants," after testing one elodea sprig once under each color. Select every valid criticism. Select all that apply.
column14: Elodea cannot carry out photosynthesis
column15: Only one kind of plant was tested, so the claim about all plants goes too far
column16: Only one sprig was used, so the result may be unusual for that sprig
column17: Only one trial was done for each color
column18: Light color should have been the dependent variable
column28: One trial, one sprig, and one species are too little evidence for a claim about all plants. Elodea does photosynthesize, and light color is correctly the independent variable. A common mistake is choosing the variable option because it sounds scientific.
column29: Ask whether the evidence is big enough to support the words "all plants."

column9: All four tubes of elodea are at 22 °C. Rank them from the FASTEST expected rate of photosynthesis to the SLOWEST.
column14: Bright lamp, water with baking soda added
column15: Bright lamp, plain water
column16: Dark closet, plain water
column17: Dim lamp, plain water
column28: The bright lamp with extra carbon dioxide has the most of both, then bright light in plain water, then dim light, then darkness, where there is no photosynthesis at all. A common mistake is thinking plain water stops photosynthesis; plain water still holds some carbon dioxide, but darkness stops photosynthesis completely, so the dark tube is last.
column29: Count how many helpful conditions each tube has: bright light, extra carbon dioxide, or neither.

column9: In a leaf disk lab, a student calculates the rate as 1 ÷ (minutes for half of the disks to float), so a shorter time gives a bigger rate. If half the disks float in 8 minutes, what is the rate?
column28: Rate = 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125 per minute. Using 1 ÷ time turns a short time into a big number, so the rate goes up when photosynthesis is faster. A common mistake is calculating 8 ÷ 1 = 8.
column29: Put the 8 on the bottom of the fraction.

column9: In a sealed chamber under a grow light, the carbon dioxide level drops from 900 ppm to 420 ppm in 2 hours. What is the average rate of carbon dioxide use, in ppm per minute?
column28: Change = 900 − 420 = 480 ppm. Time = 2 hours × 60 = 120 minutes. Rate = 480 ÷ 120 = 4 ppm per minute. A common mistake is dividing by 2 (the hours) instead of converting to 120 minutes, which gives 240.
column29: Find the drop, change the time to minutes, then divide.

column9: Counting elodea bubbles by eye can be inaccurate because some bubbles are big and some are tiny. Which change would give the most accurate measure of oxygen made?
column14: Have a different student count during each trial
column15: Collect the gas in an upside-down measuring tube and read its volume after a set time
column16: Count only the big bubbles and ignore the small ones, since tiny bubbles hold almost no oxygen
column17: Count for 10 seconds instead of 1 minute
column28: Measuring the volume of gas captures all of the oxygen, no matter the bubble size. Ignoring small bubbles loses data, a shorter count makes errors bigger, and switching counters adds a new variable. A common mistake is thinking a shorter count is more accurate.
column29: Bubble size changes, but what stays the same about the total gas?

column9: A student hypothesized that red light would give the most bubbles. Her data: red 17, blue 19, green 4, and white 20 bubbles per minute. What is the best next step?
column14: Throw out the experiment, because the prediction was wrong
column15: Change the data so red is highest
column16: Say the hypothesis was supported, because red was one of the higher colors and very close to blue
column17: Say the hypothesis was not supported, suggest why blue was also high, and repeat with more trials
column28: Red did not give the most bubbles, so the hypothesis was not supported; chlorophyll absorbs blue light strongly too. Red and blue are close, so more trials would help confirm the pattern. Changing data or claiming support anyway are the mistakes to avoid.
column29: Did red give the most bubbles? Be honest about the answer.

column9: In elodea light experiments, teachers often add a small amount of baking soda to EVERY tube, even though the experiment is testing light. Why?
column14: So the water turns blue and is easier to see
column15: Because baking soda gives the plant the light energy it needs
column16: So carbon dioxide is plentiful and not the limiting factor, letting the effect of light show
column17: Because baking soda is actually the independent variable that the light experiment is testing
column28: If carbon dioxide runs low, the plant cannot speed up no matter how bright the light gets, and the effect of light is hidden. Adding the same amount to every tube keeps carbon dioxide controlled and plentiful. A common mistake is thinking it becomes the independent variable; it is the same in every tube.
column29: If one ingredient runs short, can changing a different ingredient still show an effect?

column9: A student tests elodea at 20, 21, and 22 °C and finds no difference in bubbles per minute. What is the best way to improve the experiment?
column14: Conclude that temperature never affects photosynthesis
column15: Change the lamp brightness along with the temperature to get a bigger effect that is easier to see
column16: Test 20 °C ten more times and nothing else
column17: Test a wider range, such as 5, 15, 25, and 35 °C, so any effect is large enough to detect
column28: A 2-degree range is too small to show a clear effect, especially with bubble-counting error. A wider range tests whether temperature matters at all. A common mistake is concluding "no effect" when the test simply could not detect one.
column29: Would a 1-degree change in water feel very different to you?

column9: A cranberry grower in central Wisconsin wants to test whether a new shade netting lowers photosynthesis in the vines. Which design is best?
column14: Cover the bed nearest the road with netting and compare it with the bed next to the woods
column15: Randomly cover several beds, leave several uncovered, and measure both groups on the same days
column16: Cover every bed this year and compare the photosynthesis results with last year's uncovered beds
column17: Measure photosynthesis only in the covered beds
column28: Several randomly chosen beds in each group, measured on the same days, keep weather and location from being extra variables. Comparing two single beds, or this year with last year, mixes in location and weather. Measuring only covered beds leaves nothing to compare, which is the common mistake.
column29: A strong design has a comparison group, more than one of each, and the same timing.

column9: Elodea bubbles per minute at different water temperatures: 10 °C, 6; 20 °C, 14; 30 °C, 22; 40 °C, 9; 50 °C, 0. Select every statement supported by the data. Select all that apply.
column14: The rate rose with every increase in temperature
column15: The elodea made the most oxygen at 50 °C
column16: The rate increased from 10 °C to 30 °C
column17: Of the temperatures tested, 30 °C gave the highest rate
column28: The rate climbed to a peak of 22 at 30 °C and then fell to 9 and 0. So it did not rise with every increase, and 50 °C was the lowest, not the highest. A common mistake is reading only the first part of the table.
column29: Follow the bubble numbers in order and note where they peak.

column9: A student wants to find out whether the amount of chlorophyll in a leaf affects its rate of photosynthesis. Which experiment would work best?
column14: Measure the chlorophyll in a leaf kept in a dark closet
column15: Time how fast disks from green and pale parts of variegated leaves on one plant float, same solution and lamp
column16: Paint some leaves green and see if they make more starch
column17: Compare spinach disks and lettuce disks under two different lamps, since the two leaves differ in chlorophyll
column28: Variegated leaves have areas with more and less chlorophyll on the same plant, so chlorophyll is the only major difference when the solution and light are the same. Two plants under two lamps adds two extra variables, and paint is not chlorophyll. A common mistake is changing the plant and the light at once.
column29: Find a way to change chlorophyll while keeping the plant, light, and solution the same.

column9: Four trials at 15 cm gave 22, 24, 23, and 46 bubbles. The teacher discovers that in the 46 trial the student counted for 2 minutes instead of 1. After correcting that trial to bubbles per minute, what is the average of the four trials?
column28: The 2-minute count becomes 46 ÷ 2 = 23 bubbles per minute. Average = (22 + 24 + 23 + 23) ÷ 4 = 92 ÷ 4 = 23. A common mistake is averaging the uncorrected 46, which gives 28.75.
column29: Fix the one trial first so all four are per minute, then average.

column9: A student tests light color by placing red cellophane over one lamp and blue cellophane over an identical lamp. A light meter shows the red cellophane lets through much less light than the blue. Why is this a problem?
column14: It is not a problem, because brightness does not affect photosynthesis as long as the color is different
column15: Brightness changed along with color, so she can't blame color alone and should match the meter readings
column16: She should switch to green cellophane, which lets through the most light
column17: The light meter must be broken, because cellophane cannot block light
column28: Light color is the independent variable, so brightness must be controlled. If the red light is dimmer, fewer bubbles might come from low intensity, not from the color. Matching the meter readings fixes this. A common mistake is assuming filters change only color.
column29: Two things are different between the lamps. Which one is the one being tested?

column9: Match each problem in an elodea experiment to the best fix.
column14: The lamp heats the water when it is close :: Use an LED lamp and check the water temperature every trial
column15: The sprigs are different sizes :: Use sprigs of the same length or divide each rate by sprig mass
column16: Only one trial was run at each distance :: Run at least three trials and average them
column17: Bubbles were counted for different lengths of time :: Count for the same amount of time in every trial
column28: Each fix removes one source of unfairness: heat from the lamp, sprig size, too few trials, and uneven counting time. A common mistake is thinking more trials can fix a problem like lamp heat; repeating a flawed setup just repeats the flaw.
column29: For each problem, ask which variable is not being kept the same, or what is missing.

column9: In a temperature experiment, a student sets water baths to 10, 20, and 30 °C and checks each one with a thermometer. She argues that temperature is the dependent variable because she measured it. Which response is best?
column14: It is still the independent variable, because she set it on purpose; the thermometer only checks it
column15: She is right, because anything that is measured with a tool during an experiment is a dependent variable
column16: Temperature is a controlled variable, because it was checked every trial
column17: Temperature is the control group, because water baths were used
column28: A variable's role comes from what you do with it, not whether you measure it. She chose the temperatures, so temperature is independent; the plant's response is dependent. A common mistake is thinking anything measured must be dependent.
column29: Who decided what the temperature would be: the student or the plant?

column9: A gas syringe attached to a pondweed reads 0.0 mL at 0 minutes, 1.0 mL at 4 minutes, 2.0 mL at 8 minutes, 2.4 mL at 12 minutes, and 2.4 mL at 16 minutes. What was the rate, in mL per minute, during the first 8 minutes?
column28: In the first 8 minutes, the volume went from 0.0 to 2.0 mL, so the rate is 2.0 ÷ 8 = 0.25 mL per minute. A common mistake is using the whole 16 minutes (2.4 ÷ 16 = 0.15), which mixes in the time after the rate slowed down.
column29: Use only the readings at 0 and 8 minutes.

column9: Student 1 tests lamp distances of 10, 20, 30, and 40 cm with three trials each. Student 2 tests only 10 cm and 50 cm with ten trials each. Whose design can better show the shape of the relationship between light and photosynthesis?
column14: Student 1, because more distance levels show how the rate changes in between
column15: Student 2, because more trials always show the shape of the relationship better
column16: Neither, because distance does not affect light intensity
column17: Student 2, because the distances are farther apart, which covers a wider range of light
column28: With only two distances, you can draw only a straight line between two points and would miss a leveling off or a curve. Four levels show the pattern. Student 2's extra trials make each point more reliable, but they cannot show the shape, which is the common confusion.
column29: How many points do you need to see whether a graph curves?

column9: At 20 cm, Group 1 recorded 14, 15, and 14 bubbles per minute. Group 2 recorded 5, 28, and 12. Both averages are close to 14 or 15. Which statement is best?
column14: Group 2's data are more reliable, because they have a wider range
column15: Neither group's data can be used, because neither group got exactly the same number in all three trials
column16: Both groups are equally reliable, because their averages are almost the same, which is what matters
column17: Group 1's data are more reliable, because the trials agree; Group 2's spread suggests errors
column28: Reliable data give similar results each trial. Group 2's results jump from 5 to 28, so something was not controlled or counted well, even though the average happens to look normal. A common mistake is judging data only by the average.
column29: Look at how much each group's trials agree with each other, not just the average.

column9: A student wants to show that carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis using leaf disks. Select every part of a strong design. Select all that apply.
column14: Repeat the whole setup at least three times
column15: Use different sized cups so they are easy to tell apart
column16: The same lamp at the same distance for both cups
column17: Put the plain-water cup in the dark so the difference is bigger
column18: One cup of baking soda solution and one cup of plain water with no baking soda
column19: The same number of disks, cut from the same leaves, in each cup
column28: A strong design compares carbon dioxide vs. no added carbon dioxide while keeping light, disks, and cup size the same, and it repeats the test. Putting one cup in the dark adds light as a second variable, which is the most tempting mistake because it would make the difference bigger.
column29: Every choice should keep carbon dioxide as the only difference between the cups.
